conclusion.justification: The report explicitly answers 'Yes' to the claim, stating that offering HIV self-testing generally causes more people to test for HIV and supporting this with moderate-certainty meta-analytic evidence showing a double in testing uptake. Therefore, it strongly endorses the claim.
conclusion.label: endorses

report:
**Conclusion:** Yes. Offering HIV self-testing *in addition to, or as an alternative to,* standard HIV testing services generally causes more people to test for HIV. The strongest retrieved evidence is a 2021 systematic review/meta-analysis of 13 randomized trials: self-testing more than doubled testing uptake overall (risk ratio 2.09, 95% CI 1.69–2.58), with **moderate-certainty** evidence. A separate review likewise found a significant increase (RR 1.45, 95% CI 1.20–1.75). WHO also states that offering self-testing in facilities can increase testing uptake.

This conclusion concerns offering access to self-tests versus usual testing. It does **not** mean that supplying more than one additional kit necessarily increases testing further: one study found no difference in HIV testing when people were offered one versus two kits.

Sources:  
- https://www.thelancet.com/journals/eclinm/article/PIIS2589-5370(21)00271-6/fulltext  
- https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7713313/  
- https://www.who.int/news/item/22-07-2023-who-recommends-optimizing-hiv-testing-services  
- https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11237351/
